can: Give the numbers for each division: divisions, cells, chromosomes, alike or different.
Draw or choose the cells each division makes from a parent cell.
Explain why gametes are haploid and how independent assortment gives variation.

md: **Mitosis** is how a body cell makes two new cells. First the cell grows and **copies every chromosome exactly**. The copies line up across the middle of the cell, are pulled apart, and the cell divides **once**.

Each **daughter cell** gets one copy of every chromosome, so it has the **same number** of chromosomes and the **same genes** as the parent. Cells genetically identical to the cell they came from are **clones**. Growing, copying and dividing, again and again, is the **cell cycle**.

stem: A body cell of a pea plant has 14 chromosomes. Describe what happens to them when the cell divides by mitosis, and what the new cells hold. [3]

steps.working: The cell copies all 14 chromosomes exactly.
steps.decision: Copying comes first, so that there is a full set for each new cell.

steps.working: The copies line up across the middle, are pulled apart, and the cell divides once.
steps.decision: One copy of each chromosome goes to each side, so neither cell can end up short of one.

steps.working: Two daughter cells, each with 14 chromosomes, genetically identical to the parent: clones.
steps.decision: Same number, same genes. Nothing was halved, because each cell received a whole set.

two cells, each with 20 chromosomes, identical to each other

answer: two cells, each with 40 chromosomes, identical to the parent
explain: Mitosis copies all 40 chromosomes first, then gives one copy of each to each side, as the pea cell's 14 did in the See it. So there are two cells, each with the full 40: clones of the parent.

optionNotes.option: two cells, each with 20 chromosomes, identical to each other
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a cell splits in two, but the copying came first, so each new cell still holds all 40.

optionNotes.option: four cells, each with 40 chromosomes, all different
optionNotes.why: Four different cells is what meiosis makes; mitosis divides once, giving two cells with the parent's genes.

md: Mitosis happens in body tissues all over a plant or an animal. It does **not** make gametes: that is meiosis, in the testes and ovaries only. A cell with no nucleus, such as a red blood cell, cannot divide at all.

stem: Name the use of mitosis in each case. (a) A toddler's legs grow longer. (b) The lining of the stomach is renewed every few days. [2]

steps.working: (a) Growth.
steps.decision: More cells, each grown to full size, make a longer leg.

steps.working: (b) Replacing worn-out cells.
steps.decision: Nothing was damaged: old cells wear away and identical new ones take their place.

prompt: After a burn, new skin cells grow over the damaged area. Which use of mitosis is this?
options: repairing damaged tissue
replacing worn-out cells
growth
explain: The skin was damaged by the burn, and new cells made by mitosis fill the gap: that is repair. Replacing is for cells that wear out with no damage, as the stomach lining in the See it.

optionNotes.option: replacing worn-out cells
optionNotes.why: It tempts because new skin cells take the old ones' place, but these cells were damaged by the burn, not worn out.

optionNotes.option: growth
optionNotes.why: The body is not getting bigger here; the new cells only fill the damaged area back in.

twin.prompt: A child's arm bones lengthen year by year as she gets taller. Which use of mitosis is this?
options: growth
repairing damaged tissue
making gametes
twin.explain: Nothing is damaged or worn out: the bones gain cells and get longer, so this is growth.

optionNotes.option: repairing damaged tissue
optionNotes.why: Repair needs damage first; these bones are whole and simply getting longer.

optionNotes.option: making gametes
optionNotes.why: Gametes are made by meiosis in the testes and ovaries; mitosis never makes them.

md: **Meiosis** makes **gametes**: sperm and ova. It happens only in the **testes** and the **ovaries**. The chromosomes are copied once, then the cell divides **twice**, so one cell becomes **four**.

Each gamete gets **one chromosome from every pair**, so it has **half** the parent's number. A cell like this is **haploid**. Meiosis is a **reduction division**, because it reduces the chromosome number. The four gametes are **genetically different** from the parent and from each other.

stem: A cell in the testis of a dog has 78 chromosomes. Describe the cells meiosis makes from it. [4]

steps.working: Two divisions of the nucleus.
steps.decision: One more division than mitosis, which is what makes four cells instead of two.

steps.working: Four sperm cells from the one cell.
steps.decision: Each division doubles the cells: one, then two, then four.

steps.working: Each with 39 chromosomes, one from every pair: haploid.
steps.decision: Half of 78. A reduction division hands each gamete one member of each pair.

steps.working: All four genetically different.
steps.decision: Each holds a different mixture of the pairs, so no two sperm carry the same genes.

prompt: A cell in a sheep's ovary has 54 chromosomes and divides by meiosis. Which describes the cells it makes?
options: four cells, each with 27 chromosomes, all genetically different
four cells, each with 54 chromosomes, all genetically different
two cells, each with 27 chromosomes, genetically identical
answer: four cells, each with 27 chromosomes, all genetically different
explain: Meiosis divides twice, so one cell gives four, and each gets one chromosome from every pair: half of 54 is 27. As with the dog's 78 in the See it, the four are genetically different.

optionNotes.option: four cells, each with 54 chromosomes, all genetically different
optionNotes.why: Four cells is right, but meiosis is a reduction division: each gamete holds half the parent's 54.

optionNotes.option: two cells, each with 27 chromosomes, genetically identical
optionNotes.why: Two identical cells is mitosis's outcome; meiosis divides twice and its four cells all differ.

twin.prompt: A cell in a goat's testis has 60 chromosomes and divides by meiosis. Which describes the cells it makes?
options: four cells, each with 30 chromosomes, all different
two cells, each with 60 chromosomes, all different
four cells, each with 30 chromosomes, all identical
twin.answer: four cells, each with 30 chromosomes, all different
twin.explain: Two divisions give four cells; each has one of every pair, half of 60, so 30; and each holds a different mixture, so they differ.

optionNotes.option: two cells, each with 60 chromosomes, all different
optionNotes.why: Two cells with the full 60 is a mitosis count; meiosis gives four cells with half the number each.

optionNotes.option: four cells, each with 30 chromosomes, all identical
optionNotes.why: The count is right, but meiosis shuffles the pairs, so the four sperm are genetically different.

md: Fertilisation joins **two** gametes, one from each parent. Their chromosomes add together in the **zygote**, the first cell of the new organism.

title: Why the number must halve
md: If gametes kept the full number, every generation would have **double** the chromosomes of the one before. Halving at meiosis and adding at fertilisation cancel out, so the zygote is **diploid** again, with the parents' number, and mitosis keeps that number in every body cell.

stem: A chimpanzee's body cells have 48 chromosomes. Use numbers to explain why its gametes must hold half that number. [3]

steps.working: Without halving: 48 + 48 = 96 in the zygote.
steps.decision: Fertilisation adds the two gametes' chromosomes together.

steps.working: The next generation: 96 + 96 = 192.
steps.decision: The number would double every generation, and no two generations would match.

steps.working: With halving: 24 + 24 = 48, the same as the parents.
steps.decision: Meiosis halves, fertilisation restores: the number stays at 48 in every generation.

prompt: A pea plant's body cells have 14 chromosomes. If its gametes were not halved, how many chromosomes would a zygote have?
explain: Fertilisation adds the two gametes' chromosomes: 14 + 14 = 28, double the parent's number. That is why meiosis halves, as the chimpanzee's 48 + 48 showed in the See it.

twin.prompt: A cabbage plant's body cells have 18 chromosomes. If its gametes were not halved, how many chromosomes would a zygote have?
twin.explain: Two unhalved gametes add to 18 + 18 = 36, double the parent's 18. Meiosis halves each gamete to 9, so 9 + 9 = 18.

caption: Diploid: the chromosomes in pairs. Haploid: one chromosome from each pair.

md: Body cells hold their chromosomes in **pairs**, one of each pair from each parent: they are **diploid**. Gametes hold **one chromosome from each pair**: they are **haploid**. Mitosis makes diploid cells; meiosis makes haploid ones.

The paper often gives statements to sort: true for mitosis only, for meiosis only, or for both. Test each against the facts: divisions, cells, chromosome number, alike or different. A few fit both: each is a type of cell division, and in each the chromosomes are copied before the cell divides.

stem: Is each statement true for mitosis only, for meiosis only, or for both? (a) It produces four cells. (b) It produces diploid cells. [2]

steps.working: (a) Meiosis only.
steps.decision: Two divisions make four cells; mitosis makes two.

steps.working: (b) Mitosis only.
steps.decision: Diploid means in pairs. Mitosis keeps every pair; meiosis leaves one chromosome from each.

prompt: A statement reads: the chromosomes are copied before the cell divides. Is it true for mitosis only, for meiosis only, or for both?
options: both
mitosis only
meiosis only
explain: Both kinds of division copy the chromosomes before they divide. What differs is what happens next: mitosis divides once, meiosis twice. The See it sorted two statements that fit only one; this one fits both.

optionNotes.option: mitosis only
optionNotes.why: It tempts because mitosis is the copying division, but meiosis copies the chromosomes once before its two divisions too.

optionNotes.option: meiosis only
optionNotes.why: Copying is not what makes meiosis different; its two divisions and haploid cells are, and mitosis copies first as well.

twin.prompt: A statement reads: it produces gametes. Is it true for mitosis only, for meiosis only, or for both?
options: meiosis only
mitosis only
both
twin.explain: Gametes are made only by meiosis, in the testes and ovaries. Mitosis makes body cells for growth, replacement and repair.

optionNotes.option: mitosis only
optionNotes.why: Mitosis makes body cells; gametes need half the chromosomes, which only meiosis gives.

optionNotes.option: both
optionNotes.why: Mitosis never makes gametes: its cells keep every pair, and a gamete must hold one of each.

md: CCEA sets this as a drawing, and the marks are for what you show, not for art. For **mitosis**: **two** cells, each with **every** chromosome of the parent, in the **same combination**. Draw your chromosomes in the style the question uses.
For **meiosis**: **four** cells, each with **half** the number, **one chromosome from every pair**. Share the shaded and clear chromosomes out between the cells, so that the four differ.

stem: A cell holds a long pair and a short pair of chromosomes; in each pair one is shaded. Describe what your drawing of the cells made by meiosis must show. [4]

steps.working: Four cells.
steps.decision: Meiosis divides twice. Two cells is the mitosis answer and loses every mark that follows from it.

steps.working: Two chromosomes in each cell.
steps.decision: Half of the parent's four.

steps.working: One long and one short chromosome in each.
steps.decision: One from each pair; two long in one cell would mean a pair stayed together.

steps.working: Across the four cells, four chromosomes shaded and four clear, mixed between the cells.
steps.decision: The pairs are shared out by chance, so the cells are not all the same.

prompt: A cell has three pairs of chromosomes, six in all. What must a drawing of the cells mitosis makes from it show?
options: two cells, each with all six chromosomes as the parent has them
two cells, each with three chromosomes, one from each pair
four cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
answer: two cells, each with all six chromosomes as the parent has them
explain: Mitosis divides once and copies exactly, so the drawing shows two cells, each a match for the parent: all six chromosomes in the same combination. Halving belongs to meiosis, as the four cells of the See it did.

optionNotes.option: two cells, each with three chromosomes, one from each pair
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the cell splits in two, but halving is meiosis's mark; mitosis copies first, so each cell keeps all six.

optionNotes.option: four cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
optionNotes.why: That is the meiosis drawing, four haploid cells; mitosis gives two cells like the parent.

twin.prompt: The same cell, with three pairs of chromosomes, divides by meiosis instead. What must the drawing show?
options: four cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
four cells, each with all six chromosomes
two cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
twin.answer: four cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
twin.explain: Meiosis divides twice and halves, so the drawing shows four cells, each with three chromosomes, one from every pair.

optionNotes.option: four cells, each with all six chromosomes
optionNotes.why: Four cells is right for meiosis, but each must be haploid: one chromosome from each pair, three in all.

optionNotes.option: two cells, each with one chromosome from each pair
optionNotes.why: Half the number is right, but meiosis divides twice, so the drawing needs four cells.

md: **Higher tier.** Before the first division of meiosis, the chromosomes line up **in their pairs** across the middle of the cell. Which member of a pair faces which side is down to chance, and each pair lines up **independently** of every other pair.

This is **independent assortment**. It reassorts the chromosomes, so the gametes carry different mixtures of the parents' chromosomes. That is the source of **variation**, and when the paper asks what it does, the word variation is the mark.

title: What to let pass in the video
md: The video is made for another board, so it names the stages of meiosis and shows crossing over. CCEA states that the stages and crossing over are not required: let those parts go by.

stem: A cell has a long pair and a short pair; in each pair one chromosome is shaded. Explain how meiosis can give gametes that differ. [2]

steps.working: Line-up 1: the shaded long and the shaded short face the same side.
steps.decision: The chromosomes on each side end up in gametes together.

steps.working: Line-up 2: the shaded long faces one side and the shaded short the other.
steps.decision: Neither line-up is more likely; chance decides, pair by pair.

steps.working: So the gametes carry different mixtures of shaded and clear chromosomes: the source of variation.
steps.decision: Different mixtures in the gametes mean different offspring.

title: GCSE Biology - Meiosis (2027/28 exams)
why: Watch it for the pairs shuffling as they line up, which is the idea this section turns on.

prompt: Name the process in meiosis in which each pair of chromosomes lines up by chance, independently of the other pairs.
explain: Independent assortment: each pair lines up by chance, so the gametes get different mixtures, as the two line-ups in the See it showed. It is a cheap mark that few write.

twin.prompt: Independent assortment reassorts the chromosomes in meiosis. What does it provide in a species?
twin.explain: Variation. Different mixtures of chromosomes in the gametes mean different offspring.

md: With a long pair and a short pair, a nucleus made by meiosis needs **one long** (shaded or clear) and **one short** (shaded or clear). Each long can go with either short: 2 × 2 = **4** combinations. Each extra pair doubles the count again.

That four is not there because meiosis makes four cells. A paper may draw many nuclei and ask for every one meiosis could make: the answer is the nuclei that hold one of these combinations, whichever they are.

stem: A cell has a long pair and a short pair. Show that meiosis can make exactly four different nuclei from it. [3]

steps.working: Each nucleus takes one long chromosome: shaded or clear, 2 choices.
steps.decision: One chromosome from each pair: never both, never neither.

steps.working: Each nucleus takes one short chromosome: shaded or clear, 2 choices.
steps.decision: The short pair is sorted independently of the long pair.

steps.working: 2 × 2 = 4 combinations: shaded with shaded, shaded with clear, clear with shaded, clear with clear.
steps.decision: List them to check: every long paired with every short, nothing repeated.

prompt: A cell has three pairs of chromosomes, with one shaded member in each pair. How many different combinations could meiosis put in a nucleus?
explain: Each pair gives 2 choices, and the pairs are sorted independently, so multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. The See it's two pairs gave 2 × 2 = 4; a third pair doubles it.

twin.prompt: A cell has a long pair and a short pair. Of the combinations meiosis can make, how many hold the shaded long chromosome?
twin.explain: Fix the long as the shaded one; the short can then be shaded or clear: 2 combinations.

optionNotes.option: no: it holds only two chromosomes

**Four statements true for mitosis** (2022). Give a place for each division, then four facts about mitosis that are not true of meiosis: two cells, diploid, identical, one division. Start with skin and testes.
**Germ cells and sperm** (2023). Sperm are made by meiosis from germ cells, which are diploid and carry X and Y. Each sperm is haploid, so it carries X or Y, never both.
**Where mitosis happens** (2019). Name a type of body cell: skin, liver, a cheek cell. Never a red blood cell, which has no nucleus, and never the testes or ovaries, which are meiosis's answer.

stem: A body cell holds 18 units of DNA. Work out the DNA in each of the two cells mitosis makes from it, in a cell about to divide by meiosis, and in each gamete meiosis makes. [3]

steps.working: After mitosis: 18 units in each cell.
steps.decision: Copied to 36, then shared between two cells: back to the parent's amount.

steps.working: Before meiosis: 18 units.
steps.decision: A cell before it copies its DNA holds the same as any body cell.

steps.working: After meiosis: 9 units in each cell.
steps.decision: Half the parent's amount, as a haploid cell holds half the chromosomes.

prompt: A bar chart shows a cell holding 26 units of DNA before meiosis. Which bar height is right for each cell after meiosis?
options: 13 units
26 units
52 units
explain: Meiosis makes haploid cells with half the chromosomes, so each holds half the DNA: 26 ÷ 2 = 13. The See it's 18 became 9 the same way.

optionNotes.option: 26 units
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the bar before meiosis is 26, but meiosis halves the DNA in each cell it makes.

optionNotes.option: 52 units
optionNotes.why: 52 is the DNA just after copying, before the two divisions share it out between four cells.

twin.prompt: A cell holds 34 units of DNA before mitosis. Which bar height is right for each new cell after mitosis?
options: 34 units
17 units
68 units
twin.explain: Mitosis copies the DNA to 68 and shares it between two cells, so each new cell holds the parent's 34.

optionNotes.option: 17 units
optionNotes.why: Halving is meiosis; mitosis shares the copied DNA so each new cell has the parent's 34.

optionNotes.option: 68 units
optionNotes.why: 68 is the copied DNA before the split; each of the two new cells gets half of it.

md: A late question of six to eleven marks, usually opened by a drawing of a cell. The first mark is a number: cells, divisions or chromosomes. The last is often independent assortment and the word variation, or a comparison in full sentences. Stuck? Write the numbers for each division in the margin and answer from them.
